newsitem.title: UK: IRA would reject Major's plan - Sinn Fein leader.
newsitem.headline: IRA would reject Major's plan - Sinn Fein leader.

text.p: A leader of the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein said on Friday the guerrilla group would reject outright Britain's latest plans to establish peace in Northern Ireland.

Martin McGuinness dampened hopes of a Christmas ceasefire after Prime Minister John Major on Thursday put forward a new blueprint for getting the IRA to lay down its arms and for Sinn Fein to join all-party talks on the future of the British-ruled province.

Speaking on Britain's Channel Four television, McGuinness said: "I believe that those of us who wish to put in place a peaceful environment would have very little case indeed to go to the IRA (with Major's proposals).
"I believe that the contents of that document would be rejected outright."

Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams earlier accused Major of scuppering prospects for peace by making his terms for a truce public. "It is more than the content (that Sinn Fein objects to), it is the context," he said.
Adams and moderate Catholic leader John Hume had offered Major proposals for a new IRA ceasefire and said they wanted the negotiations to remain private until agreement was reached.

Major's statement on Thursday was his reply to these ideas, but Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said Major would have done better to wait until London and Dublin had agreed on terms before publishing anything.
Ireland launched the peace process with Britain three years ago and the governments have kept a largely united front in the search for a political solution in Northern Ireland.
Major said he was eager to get Sinn Fein into peace talks "as soon as possible" and spelled out the steps necessary for this to happen.
He said the IRA must declare a "convincing and unequivocal" ceasefire, which Sinn Fein would verify in talks with British and Irish officials.

Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew sought to smooth over the apparent disagreement between Dublin and London, ahead of a meeting between Major and Bruton on December 9 to discuss Northern Ireland.
"I notice what the Irish government have been saying, I'd like to say that I value very much the way we have been working together," he told BBC radio.

Northern Irish police earlier on Friday discovered a large bomb in a hay trailer abandoned near Armagh. The city's mayor said he believed it was intended for a British army base about half a mile (one km) away.

No group claimed responsibility, but last week a group which broke away from the IRA 10 years ago planted a bomb outside police headquarters in Northern Ireland's second city Londonderry. The army defused it after receiving a warning.
Republicans believe that by denying Sinn Fein immediate entry to talks in the event of an IRA truce, Major was bowing to political pressure from pro-British Unionists.
Major has a parliamentary majority of just one but Protestant Unionist members of parliament often vote with his government.
